messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Delivery Driver
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 48

He is seventy-seven now, a delivery driver who still knows the back roads better than most men half his age. Before the assault, he takes pride in being dependable. He wakes before dawn, drinks his coffee in the dark kitchen while his wife sleeps, and heads out with invoices tucked into a metal clipboard and a route already mapped in his mind. He likes the rhythm of the work: loading the truck, checking addresses, exchanging a few words with warehouse clerks and shop owners who have known him for years. He has always thought of himself as steady, not easily rattled.

The assault happens on an ordinary afternoon, which is part of what stays with him. He is making a delivery behind a small commercial strip, carrying a box toward a rear entrance when a man comes up fast from the alley. At first he thinks the man is asking for money or directions. Instead, the man shoves him hard, grabs at his shirt pocket, and starts yelling. He remembers the smell of stale sweat and something metallic, the shock of losing his footing, and the way the concrete rises toward him before he understands he is falling. The man kicks him while he is down and reaches for his wallet. He can hear himself grunting, can hear traffic somewhere out front continuing as if nothing unusual is happening. What frightens him later is not only the pain but the helplessness of it, the sudden knowledge that his age shows in a moment like that. By the time someone from inside hears the noise and comes out, the attacker is gone.

In the weeks afterward, he tells people he is lucky it was not worse. He has bruised ribs, a cut over one eyebrow, and a stiffness in his hip that lingers. He returns to work quickly, partly because he needs the money and partly because staying home makes him feel old. But the route no longer feels familiar. Every alley, loading dock, and half-open service door catches his eye. He starts scanning before he gets out of the truck. If he sees young men standing together near a storefront, he circles the block or skips the stop and comes back later. He keeps the engine running when he can. He tells himself these are sensible precautions, yet his hands shake when he reaches for the parking brake.

At night, his wife notices the change before he admits it. He jerks awake sweating, sometimes halfway out of bed, breathing as though he has been running. When she touches his shoulder, he flinches first and recognizes her second. He dreams of being on the ground, unable to get air into his chest, while footsteps come closer. Some nights the dream is so vivid he gets up and checks that the doors are locked, then checks again twenty minutes later because he cannot remember if he really did. He has always been a sociable man, but now he sits with his back to the wall in diners and watches the entrance instead of joining the conversation.

What troubles him most is the humiliation. He does not talk about the assault in detail because he feels he should have handled it differently. He replays it while driving, bargaining with the past: if he had noticed the alley sooner, if he had not carried the box alone, if he had fought harder. In those moments he grips the steering wheel until his knuckles pale. A car backfiring or a stranger raising his voice in a parking lot can send a bolt through him so suddenly that he feels weak and furious at the same time. He snaps at his wife over small things and then goes quiet, ashamed. He used to stop and chat with receiving clerks; now he drops the package, gets the signature, and leaves.

He has also begun turning down routes that involve unfamiliar neighborhoods, though he explains it as wanting less wear on the truck. His world grows smaller in ways he does not intend. He avoids the part of town where the assault happened. If dispatch changes his schedule without warning, he feels his stomach tighten and starts imagining where he might be cornered. He notices every person lingering near the rear of a building. Even on days that go smoothly, his body never fully stands down. By the time he gets home, he is exhausted from the vigilance of it.

He speaks about all this carefully, almost apologetically, because he has spent a lifetime believing men endure what happens and keep moving. Yet as he describes his days now, it becomes clear how much of each one is organized around the assault. The route that once gave him pleasure has become a chain of calculations about danger. Home is safer, but not entirely restful. He still drives, still works, still puts on his boots each morning before sunrise. But the ordinary world he trusted to stay ordinary has not fully returned.
